title: Clients vs. customers
body: Your client, the principal, gets full fiduciary duties. A customer is the other party you aren't representing. They get honesty and fair dealing, but not your loyalty or advice.
example: A Henderson listing agent's client is the seller. The unrepresented buyer who calls on the sign is a customer.
hook: Clients get loyalty. Customers get honesty.

title: Universal, general, special
body: A universal agent can do anything the principal can. A general agent handles a range of matters in one business. A special agent does one specific job. A listing broker is a special agent of the seller.
example: A Las Vegas property manager collecting rent and hiring vendors for an owner is a general agent.
hook: Universal: all. General: a business. Special: one task.

title: Dual, assigned, and subagency
body: Dual agency means one agent or firm represents both sides; it needs informed written consent where allowed. Assigned (designated) agency puts different licensees on each side within one firm. A subagent works for the listing broker on the seller's behalf.
example: Two agents at the same Reno brokerage each represent one side, with the broker supervising both.
hook: Two clients, one firm: disclose and get consent.

title: How agency starts
body: Agency is created by express agreement, implied by conduct, by ratification after the fact, or by estoppel when a principal makes a third party believe someone is their agent.
example: A Carson City owner says nothing while a broker markets the home, then accepts the broker's buyer. That can ratify the agency.
hook: Agreement, actions, approval after, or appearances.

title: How agency ends
body: Agency ends by performance, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation by the principal, renunciation by the agent, or by law: death, incapacity, bankruptcy, or destruction of the property.
example: A Las Vegas seller's house sells and closes. The listing agency ends by performance.
hook: Done, expired, agreed, fired, quit, or law.

title: Agency coupled with an interest
body: If the agent owns an interest in the property, the principal can't revoke the agency, and it doesn't end when the principal dies.
example: A broker who co-owns a Henderson lot with the seller holds an agency coupled with an interest.
hook: Own a piece, can't be fired.

title: The fiduciary duties: OLDCAR
body: An agent owes the principal Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, and Reasonable care. These go to clients, not customers.
example: A Reno buyer's agent keeps the buyer's top price secret, reports every offer, and tracks the earnest money.
hook: OLDCAR: the six things a client is owed.

title: Obedience and loyalty, with limits
body: Follow the client's lawful instructions and put their interests first. Never follow an unlawful instruction, such as refusing to show to a protected class or hiding a known defect.
example: A Las Vegas seller says don't show to families with kids. The agent refuses; that's illegal discrimination.
hook: Obey the lawful. Refuse the unlawful.

title: Disclosure, confidentiality, accounting
body: Tell your client every material fact you learn. Keep their private information private, even after the agency ends. Account for every dollar you hold for them.
example: A Henderson buyer's agent learns the seller is in foreclosure and must close fast. The agent tells the buyer.
hook: Tell your client everything. Tell others nothing private.

title: Duties to everyone
body: Even to customers, licensees must be honest, deal fairly, and disclose known material defects. Caveat emptor no longer protects a licensee who stays silent about a known problem.
example: A Reno listing agent knows the roof leaks. They must disclose it to buyers even though the buyers aren't their clients.
hook: Honest with everyone. Loyal to your client.

title: Fraud, negligence, puffing
body: Fraud is an intentional lie about a material fact. Negligent misrepresentation is a false statement made carelessly. Puffing is obvious opinion, like "gorgeous views," and isn't actionable unless it states a false fact.
example: Saying a Summerlin home has "the best kitchen on the block" is puffing. Saying it has a new roof when it doesn't is misrepresentation.
hook: Opinion is puffing. False fact is trouble.

title: Advice you can't give
body: Licensees must not give legal or tax advice, and must not claim expertise they lack. Recommend an attorney, CPA, inspector, or other expert when a question goes beyond real estate brokerage.
example: A Henderson seller asks how to minimize capital gains. The agent refers them to a CPA.
hook: Know your lane. Refer the rest.

title: Disclose who you represent
body: State law requires telling the parties in writing whom you represent, at a set time and on required forms. Disclosure protects consumers and the licensee.
example: Nevada requires its own agency disclosure forms. You'll learn them in the Nevada units.
hook: Say who you work for before they say too much.

title: Conflicts of interest
body: Disclose any personal interest in a deal: buying a listing yourself, selling to a relative, or getting a referral fee. Undisclosed conflicts, secret profits, and self-dealing breach loyalty.
example: A Las Vegas agent wants to buy a client's home. The agent discloses in writing that they're the buyer and that they're licensed.
hook: If it benefits you, disclose it.

title: Undisclosed dual agency
body: Representing both sides without telling them and getting consent is one of the most serious agency violations. It can cost the commission, bring discipline, and expose the licensee to lawsuits.
example: A Reno agent quietly advises both buyer and seller on price. Both can claim breach of loyalty.
hook: Secret dual agency: two clients, zero loyalty.
